newsitem.title: JAPAN: Thousand-boat task force to tackle Japan oil spill.
newsitem.headline: Thousand-boat task force to tackle Japan oil spill.

text.p: Japan plans to put together a motley fleet of 1,000 boats of all types to tackle spreading environmental damage from the country's worst oil spill, government officials said on Monday.

Transport Minister Makoto Koga said the vessels, which would include small fishing boats and any other volunteer private craft would join government ships in an all-out effort to beat back the 18-day-old spill from a sunken Russian tanker.
The polluted area is dotted with shellfish farms, scenic beaches and marine bird sanctuaries along a 900-km (560-mile) stretch of coastline about 300 km (190 miles) west of Tokyo.
Koga told reporters the effort would be a hand-to-hand battle and anyone was welcome to join in.
"In order to get rid of the oil as fast as possible we have to use the extremely unscientific, but most effective method of collection by hand," Koga said.
"I am asking for sincere action from all boat owners."

The fleet -- a massive step up from 66 government ships and small numbers of fishing boats currently engaged in the clean-up -- would be sent to clean up slicks threatening vital feeding grounds for fish and shellfish along the northern Japan coast as well as the world's biggest concentration of nuclear power plants at Wakasa Bay.
"The plan is to gather over 1,000 boats together to mount an oil cleaning operation to protect areas which also have not yet been affected by oil slicks," a Transport Ministry spokesman said.
"We don't know how fast it can happen but we want it as quickly as possible," he added.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters after an oil disaster meeting of 15 cabinet ministers, including heads of the Foreign Ministry, Defense Agency and Environment Agency, that a cabinet-level approach was needed to deal with the incident.
"There is now great reason to fear for the effect on the environment and fisheries... Central government help is necessary to deal with the problem," Kajiyama said.

Shortly after the cabinet meeting, local officials in Akita Prefecture in the far north of Japan's main island of Honshu reported oil had washed ashore there, implying that seven of Japan's 47 prefectures had been affected.

A six-km (four-mile)-long floating streak of oil continued to lengthen near where the stern portion of the tanker Nakhodka broke into two in a storm and sank in the Sea of Japan on January 2, some 130 km (80 miles) off the coast of Shimane Prefecture.
The stern section carried most of the 19,000-tonne (133,000-barrel) cargo of heavy oil on the 13,157-tonne vessel.
But most pollution so far has been caused by the bow of the ship, which went aground on rocks near the fishing village of Mikuni in Fukui Prefecture.
The 31-man crew was rescued but the captain was missing presumed drowned.
